extracted.intended_audience: journalists (especially education reporters covering LGBTQ students)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for journalists on language, interviewing practices, sourcing, data and resources when covering LGBTQ people — with an emphasis on students and education reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer your pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering your pronouns — e.g. she/her/hers, they/them/theirs — at the start of a conversation invites your interviewee to reply with the information they want you to have about their identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your own pronouns to signal openness and allow sources to provide the identity information they prefer; treat this as an invitation rather than an imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not interview minors alone when avoidable
rubrics_metrics.description: Young people don’t always make good decisions about sharing information. If possible, have a parent present. If that’s inadvisable, perhaps a school’s gay-straight alliance adviser or another trusted adult can be tapped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on minors, arrange for a guardian or trusted adult to be present unless doing so would create danger or prevent the story; be mindful of safety and consent concerns. The page notes a practitioner preference to avoid talking to children alone in hostile contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ask about anatomy or medical transition details
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s almost never appropriate to ask about a person’s anatomy or the medical details of their transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid invasive medical questions; focus on aspects of the story that are relevant and consented to by the source. Medical details are generally private and often irrelevant to reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid referring to a person’s biology in politically charged terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Because an evolving base of scientific knowledge has identified sex and gender as complicated and not necessarily fixed, it’s also inappropriate — and politically charged — to refer to a person’s biology, e.g. “biologically male.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the language and identity terms the person uses; avoid biological shorthand that mischaracterizes gender identity or inflames political debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctly contextualize medical facts about minors
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to heated rhetoric, gender-confirmation surgery is generally not performed on minors. Puberty-suppressing drugs are fully reversible and temporarily stop the development of permanent secondary sex characteristics, such as Adam’s apples and breasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to correct common misconceptions and report medical facts accurately when relevant; consult reputable medical sources and include contextualizing information to avoid spreading misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not deadname people
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not “deadname,” or use the pre-transition name, of a transgender person unless they invite you to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always use the name the person currently uses unless there's a compelling, clearly explained reason (and consent) to do otherwise; explain editorial choices when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult established LGBTQ style guides
rubrics_metrics.description: There are numerous LGBTQ style guides for journalists... AP Stylebook created its Transgender Coverage Topical Guide in 2022. NLGJA ... offers a style guide and a “toolbox” with guidance on journalistic issues... The GLAAD Media Reference Guide has helpful information... Trans Journalists Association provides a style guide...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative guides (AP, NLGJA, GLAAD, Trans Journalists Association, etc.) as primary references for terminology, red flags, and recommended practice; be aware some resources may require sign-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure balance while avoiding sensational or discredited storylines
rubrics_metrics.description: NLGJA: guidance on journalistic issues, such as ensuring balance while avoiding sensational but discredited storylines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for fair reporting that does not amplify sensational, debunked narratives; seek multiple credible sources and contextual evidence rather than false balance that elevates fringe claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid citing 'fringe' or discredited experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Trans Journalists Association cautions about supposed experts most qualified professionals consider “fringe” sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vet expert sources for credibility within the relevant medical, psychological, or social-science communities; avoid amplifying voices that lack mainstream professional endorsement when presenting expert claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve representation of gender-nonconforming people in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Trans Journalists Association style guide includes ... suggestions for improving representation of gender-nonconforming people in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek inclusive, respectful portrayals and avoid tokenism; include diverse perspectives from within the community and depict lived experiences accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reputable data sources but note limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Note: Data has limitations, but there’s increasingly available data. (List includes CDC Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System; GLSEN school climate survey; Movement Advancement Project; NFHS athletic participation; RAND panels; Trevor Project Survey; Williams Institute; U.S. Trans Survey; Census Household Pulse Survey; OCR Open Investigations.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on established surveys and institutional datasets for background and context, but acknowledge sampling and measurement limitations; cross-check multiple sources where possible and cite methodology when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for stories using public records and local documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where to Look: Legal filings, Municipal/district-specific health and youth/student experience surveys and assessments... legislation and written policy language; School board hours and records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public records, local policies, school board minutes, and district surveys to uncover stories and verify claims; search municipal and district-specific documents for angles not visible in national coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate teachers’ voices and workforce research
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting Teachers on the Record — advice on how to incorporate teachers’ voices in coverage. Finding Data to Cover the Teacher Workforce — lists organizations providing research and data on the teacher workforce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include perspectives of educators while understanding their unique challenges and constraints; use workforce and contract data to contextualize reporting on schools and staff.
